title: Non-viral in situ gene editing effectively and safely rescues congenital ichthyosis-causing mutations in human skin
projectDescription: Autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) refers to a group of rare, highly debilitating skin disorders which significantly impair patients’ quality of life and lack any effective treatment options.  Here, we report clinically-relevant in situ correction of the most common ARCI-causing mutation TGM1 c.877-2A>G, a splice-site aberration, in human disease models. Targeted skin barrier modulation followed by topical application of the cytosine base editor eTD packaged into lipid nanoparticles yielded functional restoration of ~30% of wild-type transglutaminase 1 activity in skin tissue.  Toxicity studies and comprehensive off-target analysis demonstrated an excellent safety profile even after repeated application, without systemic distribution of the lipid nanoparticles or the genetic cargo as determined via highly-sensitive methods including DESI metabolic imaging.  This study presents comprehensive preclinical data on the feasibility of in situ gene correction of genodermatoses-causing mutations showcasing its therapeutic potential and paving the way for curative next-generation treatments for severe genetic skin diseases.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Laser microdissection and proteomic sample preparation 3D ARCI skin disease models were collected and prepared for proteomics analysis 7 days post-editing. For laser microdissection, tissue sections were stained with H&E as described previously on PPS-Membrane Frame Slides. For each sample, we collected an area of 0.04 mm2. We utilized the Leica LMD7 system along with LMD software version 8.3.0.08259. Tissue collection was performed using a 20X objective (HC PL FL L 20x/0.40 CORR) in brightfield, with laser settings as follows: power at 60, aperture at 1, speed at 20, middle pulse count at 1, final pulse at –1, and head current between 40-70% (adjusted according to tissue thickness), with a pulse frequency of approximately 2000. Contours were gathered in low-binding 384-well plates (Eppendorf 0030129547). To ensure the tissue settled at the bottom of each well, 20μL of acetonitrile was added, followed by brief vortexing and vacuum drying for 10 minutes at 60 °C. Visual inspection was conducted afterward to confirm successful collection. Protein extraction and digestion were carried out using a DDM-based protocol. A lysis buffer containing 0.025% DDM, 5 mM TCEP, 20 mM CAA, and 0.1 M TEAB in water was dispensed into each well (4 μL per sample) using a MANTIS Liquid Dispenser. Plates were sealed with PCR ComfortLid seals and incubated at 95 °C for 60 minutes. After cooling, 2μL of LysC (4 ng/μL in 0.1 M TEAB [pH 8.5] with 30% acetonitrile) was added, and samples were digested for 4 hours at 37 °C in a thermal cycler. Subsequently, 3μL of trypsin (2ng/μL in 0.1 M TEAB [pH 8.5] with 10% acetonitrile) was added, and digestion continued overnight at 37 °C. The following day, samples were vacuum dried in preparation for peptide cleanup. Peptides were purified using Evotips (Evosep) according to the manufacturer's instructions, and samples were stored with Buffer A until measurement.  Liquid chromatography-based mass spectrometry (LC–MS) analysis  LC-MS analysis was performed on an Evosep ONE (Evosep Biosystems) LC system connected to a trapped ion mobility spectrometry quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer (timsTOF Ultra 2, Bruker Daltonics). The Evosep ONE was operated in the Whisper Zoom configuration and was used with an Aurora Elite (15 cm x 75 µm x 1.7 µm, IonOpticks) column at 50°C. Buffer A consists of 0.1% formic acid in LC-MS grade water and buffer B is 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile. Peptides were separated with Whisper Zoom 40SPD method. Eluted peptides were measured in dia-PASEF mode Capillary voltage was set to 1750 V with a capillary temperature of 200 °C. The MS method consisted of eight MS/MS PASEF cycles with fixed 25 Da windows from 400 – 1000 m/z in an ion mobility range between 0.64 – 1.37 1/k0 with 100 ms accumulation and ramping time at a cycle time of 0.95 s.
dataProcessingProtocol: Proteomics Raw File Processing  DIA-NN125 Academic (version 2.0) was employed for the analysis of raw files. To create DIA-NN in silico predicted libraries, the human FASTA file and commonly encountered contaminants 126 (UP000005640_9606, downloaded on March 6th, 2025) were used. DIA-NN was run in its default mode with slight modifications. In summary, the precursor false discovery rate (FDR) was set at 1%, with precursor charge states ranging from 2 to 4, and a precursor m/z range of 300 to 1000. The MS1 and MS2 accuracies were 15.0 ppm, and scan windows were set to 0 (assigned by DIA-NN). Both MBR and protein inference were activated. Oxidation (M) and acetyl (Protein-N-term) were considered as variable modifications, while carbamidomethyl (C) was a fixed modification, allowing a maximum of two modifications per peptide. The report.pg matrix output file from DIA-NN was utilized for further data analysis, applying a global protein q-value threshold of 1%. Proteomics Data Analysis  Proteomics data analysis was performed with Perseus127 (versions 1.6.5.0). Prior differential abundance analysis, data was filtered for at least 70% valid values in at least one experimental group. The remaining missing values were imputed by low-abundance normal distribution per protein (width=0.3, downshift=1.8). Pairwise proteomic comparisons (two-sided t-test) were performed including a permutation-based false discovery rate of 5%. For heatmap visualizations and data matrix exports, InstantClue 128 was used. Peptide intensities corresponding to TGM1 were grouped by position relative to the truncation site (N-terminal = before; C-terminal = after); group differences were tested with t-tests with Bonferroni correction. For pathway analysis, proteins significant at FDR q ≤ 0.05 were ranked by the log2 fold change and the top 100 proteins with higher abundance for each contrast were submitted to Enrichr for over-representation analysis against GO: Biological Process.
